explanation: What is ordinary at home may be rude elsewhere, and the other way round. The proverb teaches you not to judge foreign habits by your own yardstick, but to understand them first.
example_usage: “In Japan he was startled to find that tipping isn't done at all. So many countries, so many customs.”
origin: From the Latin “quot regiones, tot mores”; attested in English since the 16th century.

text: Řekni mi, kdo jsou tví přátelé, a já ti řeknu, kdo jsi ty.
meaning: Člověka poznáš podle společnosti, kterou vyhledává.
explanation: Přátele si vybíráme podle toho, co sami ceníme — a jejich vliv nás pak dál utváří. Přísloví nabízí spolehlivé měřítko charakteru tam, kde slova nestačí.
example_usage: „Chodí výhradně s lidmi, kteří pomáhají v útulku. Řekni mi, kdo jsou tví přátelé, a já ti řeknu, kdo jsi ty.“
origin: Ze španělského „Dime con quién andas, y te diré quién eres“, proslaveného Cervantesovým Donem Quijotem (1615).

text: Tell me what company you keep and I will tell you who you are.
meaning: A person is known by the company they choose.
explanation: We pick friends by what we value — and their influence then shapes us further. The proverb offers a reliable measure of character where words fall short.
example_usage: “All her friends volunteer at the shelter too. Tell me what company you keep and I will tell you who you are.”
origin: From the Spanish “Dime con quién andas, y te diré quién eres”, made famous by Cervantes's Don Quixote (1615).

text: Chléb padne vždy namazanou stranou dolů.
meaning: Když se něco nepovede, pokazí se to tím nejnepříjemnějším způsobem.
explanation: Smolné události jako by si vybíraly nejhorší možnou variantu. Přísloví je žertovným povzdechem nad smůlou — a tichou radou počítat i s tou nejotravnější možností.
example_usage: „Upadl mu telefon a dopadl přesně displejem na dlažbu. Chléb padne vždy namazanou stranou dolů.“
origin: Anglické rčení doložené od 19. století; zlidovělo jako lidová obdoba Murphyho zákona.

text: The bread never falls but on its buttered side.
meaning: When something goes wrong, it goes wrong in the most annoying way possible.
explanation: Bad luck seems to pick the worst available option every time. The proverb is a wry sigh at misfortune — and quiet advice to expect the most irritating outcome.
example_usage: “He dropped his phone and it landed screen-first on the pavement. The bread never falls but on its buttered side.”
origin: English saying attested since the 19th century, a folk forerunner of Murphy's law.

meaning: Nejméně víme o tom, co se děje přímo u nás.
explanation: Svíce osvětluje dálku, ale vlastní patu nechává ve stínu. Přísloví vystihuje slepotu vůči blízkému — problémy doma či ve vlastní firmě si všimneme nejpozději.
example_usage: „Roky školil firmy o kybernetické bezpečnosti a vlastní účet měl bez dvoufázového ověření. Pod svícnem bývá největší tma.“
origin: Evropské přísloví doložené v mnoha jazycích; v češtině zlidovělé z lidové tradice.

text: The darkest place is under the candlestick.
meaning: We know least about what happens right under our noses.
explanation: A candle lights the distance but leaves its own base in shadow. The proverb captures blindness to the near at hand — trouble at home or in one's own firm is noticed last.
example_usage: “He taught cybersecurity for years and never enabled two-factor on his own account. The darkest place is under the candlestick.”
origin: A European proverb found in many languages; attested in English since the 17th century.

text: Kdo drbe s tebou, bude drbat i tebe.
meaning: Kdo před tebou pomlouvá druhé, pomluví i tebe.
explanation: Ochota mluvit o nepřítomných se nezastaví u jednoho člověka — je to povahový rys, ne jednorázová výjimka. Přísloví radí být ostražitý vůči tomu, kdo nás zásobuje klepy.
example_usage: „Vyprávěla mi o všech kolegyních — a mně pak došlo, že o mně určitě mluví taky. Kdo drbe s tebou, bude drbat i tebe.“
origin: Přísloví španělského původu, zapsané v anglických sbírkách od 17. století.

text: Who chatters to you will chatter of you.
meaning: Whoever gossips to you about others will gossip about you.
explanation: A willingness to talk about the absent does not stop at one person — it is a trait, not a one-off exception. The proverb advises wariness toward anyone who supplies you with gossip.
example_usage: “She told me everything about our colleagues, and then it hit me that she surely talks about me too. Who chatters to you will chatter of you.”
origin: A proverb of Spanish origin, recorded in English collections since the 17th century.

meaning: Zaběhnuté návyky se v pozdním věku mění jen těžko.
explanation: Po letech opakování se způsoby stanou druhou přirozeností a učit se jinak stojí nesrovnatelně víc sil. Přísloví to konstatuje — ale bývá i pohodlnou výmluvou.
example_usage: „Nabídli mu školení na nový systém a on zůstal u svého sešitu. Starého psa novým kouskům nenaučíš.“
origin: Anglické přísloví doložené ve sbírce Nathana Baileyho Divers Proverbs (1721); v češtině zdomácnělé.

text: You can't teach an old dog new tricks.
meaning: Settled habits are very hard to change late in life.
explanation: After years of repetition, ways become second nature and relearning costs incomparably more effort. The proverb states this plainly — though it also serves as a convenient excuse.
example_usage: “They offered him training on the new system and he stuck to his paper ledger. You can't teach an old dog new tricks.”
origin: Recorded in Nathan Bailey's Divers Proverbs (1721), from the older form “an old dog will learn no tricks”.

text: A fish rots from the head down.
meaning: An organisation's decay begins with its leadership.
explanation: What is rotten at the top seeps downward. The proverb looks for the cause of decline where the power and responsibility sit — at the head, not in the body.
example_usage: “The directors were expensing holidays, so nobody was surprised when the warehouse started losing stock. A fish rots from the head down.”
origin: A Greek saying recorded by Erasmus in his Adagia; proverbial in English since the 16th century.

meaning: A lie cannot travel far before it collapses.
explanation: Falsehood has nothing to stand on, so it needs constant propping up until it finally gives way. The proverb warns that lying is a short-term strategy with a certain end.
example_usage: “He claimed he'd been at the conference until someone posted a photo of him at the match. A lie has no legs.”
origin: English saying attested since the 17th century, often in the fuller form “a lie has no legs, but a scandal has wings”.

meaning: Those who arrive first get served first.
explanation: The fairest rule where goods are scarce is the simplest one: order of arrival. The proverb both states the custom and rewards promptness.
example_usage: “There are twenty places on the course and no reservations — first come, first served.”
origin: From the medieval milling rule, as in Chaucer's “whoso first cometh to the mille, first grynt” (14th century).

meaning: Nothing beautiful comes without a drawback.
explanation: Beauty and pain grow on a single stem. The proverb reconciles us to the fact that everything valuable — love, work, success — carries its thorns as well.
example_usage: “The dream job abroad also meant missing every family birthday. No rose without a thorn.”
origin: A medieval European proverb from the Latin “nulla rosa sine spinis”, with roots in Persian poetry.

text: Patience and time overcome all things.
meaning: Steady endurance achieves what force cannot.
explanation: Some obstacles yield to no amount of strength, only to persistence applied over time. The proverb recommends waiting and working rather than forcing.
example_usage: “It took her four years of appeals, but the ruling was finally overturned. Patience and time overcome all things.”
origin: From La Fontaine's fable line “patience et longueur de temps font plus que force ni que rage” (17th century).

text: The pitcher goes so often to the well that it is broken at last.
meaning: Repeated risk-taking eventually ends badly.
explanation: What worked a hundred times need not work the hundred-and-first, and wear accumulates unseen. The proverb warns that getting away with a risk is only ever temporary.
example_usage: “He drove home after a drink for years until the night he lost his licence. The pitcher goes so often to the well that it is broken at last.”
origin: A medieval European proverb, attested in English since the 14th century (John Gower).

text: Kdo si počká, ten se dočká.
meaning: Trpělivé čekání se nakonec vyplatí.
explanation: Některé věci nelze uspěchat — zrají vlastním tempem a přijdou samy, když je čas. Přísloví povzbuzuje k trpělivosti tam, kde netrpělivost nic neurychlí.
example_usage: „Tři roky byla na pořadníku a byt nakonec dostala. Kdo si počká, ten se dočká.“
origin: České lidové přísloví s obdobami po celé Evropě.

meaning: Kdo vstává a jedná brzy, dosáhne víc.
explanation: Ráno patří tomu, kdo je vzhůru — má klid, náskok i volné pole. Přísloví chválí ranní píli jako tichou výhodu, která se za den nastřádá.
example_usage: „Chodí do dílny v šest a v poledne má hotovo, co ostatní stíhají do večera. Ranní ptáče dál doskáče.“
origin: České lidové přísloví; obdobu o ranním ptáku zná i angličtina od 17. století.
